RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Hibernians in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Hill of Tara & Gaelic Tuaths, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Hibernians was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Hill of Tara & Gaelic Tuaths, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Drovers push the cattle down the lane toward the hill fort, and a spearman guards the herd against thieves waiting in the bracken. Pay comes in cattle, bronze, and a few gold rings, and a warrior who loses the herd loses his share as well. He would rather fight a rival clan than walk home with an empty fold.

The royal reeve tallies the cattle brought to Tara and marks which tuath owes tribute. Hides, butter, and iron go to the fair at the hill, and the high king takes his cut before the chieftains divide the rest. Every cow recorded in the reeve's book is a claim that a neighbor may one day dispute.
